subject: biology
title: Variation: genes, environment and phenotype
key_idea: Phenotypic variation is caused by genes, by the environment, or by both. Discontinuous variation has distinct categories and is controlled by one or a few genes. Continuous variation has a full range of values and is controlled by many genes, called polygenic inheritance, plus the environment.

blocks.text: Individuals of the same species differ in their phenotype. The differences have three possible causes.

rows: Genetic
Different alleles are inherited
ABO blood group; sex; flower colour in peas
Environmental
Conditions during life change the phenotype
A scar; a language spoken; a plant grown in the dark
Both
Genes set the limits; the environment decides where in the range an individual ends up
Height, body mass, skin colour

blocks.text: Two identical twins have the same genotype. Differences between them are mainly caused by the environment.

items: Diet affects body mass and growth in animals, whatever alleles they carry.
A plant grown without light grows long and pale (**etiolation**), though its genes are the same as a plant grown in the light.
Sun exposure darkens skin, but only within the range the genes allow.
Variation is genetic, environmental or a combination of the two.
Genes set the potential; the environment affects how much of it is expressed.
Differences between identical twins are mainly caused by the environment.

blocks.text: Phenotypes vary in two ways. The type of variation tells you how many genes are involved.

sections.heading: The genetic basis of each type

blocks.text: The number of genes involved is the main difference. This is the reason for the shape of the data.

items: Controlled by **one gene** or a small number of genes, each with different alleles.
Each genotype gives one of a few distinct phenotypes.
The environment has little or no effect. A person is blood group A whatever they eat.
Controlled by **many genes** at different loci. This is **polygenic inheritance**.
Each gene has a small additive effect, and each locus can carry different alleles.
Many different genotype combinations give many different phenotypes, with all values in between.
The environment also has a large effect, which blurs the steps between genotypes.
Most individuals are near the mean, so a histogram is a bell-shaped (normal) curve.

diagram.prompt: Is each characteristic continuous or discontinuous?

items.text: Leaf length in one tree species

items: One or few genes give discontinuous variation; many genes give continuous variation.
Polygenic means many genes, each with a small effect.
The environment adds to continuous variation, so it forms a smooth range.

checks.q: Explain why human height shows continuous variation.
checks.a: Height is controlled by many genes (polygenic inheritance), each with a small additive effect. The environment, such as diet, also affects it. So there is a full range of heights between the extremes, rather than distinct categories.

checks.q: ABO blood group shows discontinuous variation. Give two features of this type of variation.
checks.a: Any two from: distinct categories with no intermediates; controlled by one gene (or a few genes); little or no effect of the environment.

checks.q: Two seedlings with the same genotype are grown, one in the light and one in the dark. The one in the dark is taller and paler. Explain this difference.
checks.a: The genotype is the same, so the difference is caused by the environment (the amount of light). Growth in the dark is etiolated: the plant grows tall and pale to reach light.

blocks.text: Some phenotypes are affected by several alleles at many loci, together with the environment. You need to link this to continuous variation.

items: Each locus may have more than one allele, and each allele adds a small effect to the phenotype.
The effects of many loci add together, giving a large number of possible phenotypes.
Because the environment also acts, the data fit a smooth, bell-shaped curve.

blocks.text: A gene codes for a protein, and the protein produces the phenotype. Know the pathway for each of these four examples.

rows: TYR gene: the enzyme tyrosinase
Mutant alleles code for a non-functional enzyme
Albinism: no melanin is made, so skin, hair and eyes lack pigment (recessive)
HBB gene: the β-globin polypeptide of haemoglobin
A base substitution changes one amino acid (glutamic acid to valine)
Sickle cell anaemia: haemoglobin forms fibres at low oxygen and red blood cells sickle (recessive)
F8 gene: factor VIII, a blood clotting protein
A mutation gives non-functional factor VIII
Haemophilia: blood clots slowly (X-linked recessive)
HTT gene: huntingtin protein
A longer than normal run of repeated bases gives an abnormal protein
Huntington's disease: the protein damages nerve cells in the brain, usually in adulthood (dominant)

items: **Gibberellin** is a plant hormone that stimulates stem elongation.
The dominant allele **Le** codes for a functional enzyme in the gibberellin synthesis pathway.
The recessive allele **le** codes for a non-functional enzyme, so less active gibberellin is made.
LeLe and Lele plants make enough gibberellin and grow tall. lele plants are short (dwarf).
Giving gibberellin to a dwarf plant makes it grow tall, which shows the cause is a lack of the hormone.
An allele that changes a protein can change the phenotype.
A non-functional enzyme usually gives a recessive allele.
Le is dominant because one functional copy of the enzyme is enough.

items.meaning: Differences between individuals of the same species.
Differences between members of different species.

blocks.text: Examples cover plants, animals and microorganisms, with genetic and environmental causes.

items: Plants: seed shape in peas is genetic. Etiolation in the dark is environmental.
Animals: body mass varies with genes and with diet.
Microorganisms: bacteria differ in antibiotic resistance (genetic) and in colony size with nutrient supply (environmental).

blocks.text: How sexual reproduction creates genetic variation

items: In meiosis, crossing over swaps alleles between homologous chromosomes.
Independent assortment sends maternal and paternal chromosomes into gametes at random.
Random fusion of gametes at fertilisation joins any sperm to any egg, giving a different combination of alleles each time.

blocks.text: Continuous variation involves many genes; discontinuous variation involves one or a small number of genes.
